analytic.title: Conditionally Optimal Task Parallelization for Global EDF on Multi-core Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Targeting global EDF scheduling, this paper proposes a conditionally optimal algorithm for parallelizing tasks with parallelization freedom. For this, we extend the interferencebased sufficient schedulability analysis and derive monotonic increasing properties of both tolerance and interference for the schedulability. Leveraging those properties, we propose a oneway search based conditionally optimal algorithm with polynomial time complexity. Our extensive experiments through both simulation and actual implementation show that our proposed approach can significantly improve the schedulability up to 60 percent.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recent parallel computing frameworks, such as OpenCL [1] and OpenMP [2], allow us to parallelize a real-time task in many different ways, which is called "parallelization freedom". For example, a lane-tracking program can be executed as a single thread, two threads, three threads, and four threads as shown in Fig. 1. Depending on how to parallelize it, its thread execution times significantly vary, that is, more parallelization tends to reduce each thread execution time but increase the total execution time due to parallelization overheads.

In these frameworks with parallelization freedom, to better utilize the multiple CPU cores for maximizing the schedulability, we have to carefully determine a "parallelization option" of each task, i.e., the number of threads the task gets parallelized into. Recent works [3], [4] address the parallelization option assignment problem targeting fluid scheduling such as PD 2 [5] and LLREF [6]. However, fluid scheduling is hardly practical due to a massive number of scheduling invocations and context switches. For more widely used global EDF scheduling, G-EDF for short, the concept of parallelization freedom still has not brought much attention. Thus, this paper proposes a way of optimally assign parallelization options to real-time tasks for G-EDF on a multi-core system. Moreover, we aim to propose a polynomial time algorithm that can be used for online situations where tasks dynamically join and leave.

To assign parallelization options to tasks, we have to check whether an assignment solution makes tasks schedulable. Therefore, the problem of the parallelization option assignment is, at least, as complex as the schedulability analysis itself. Moreover, combined with the sheer number of possible combinations of parallelization options, the problem space can grow exponentially. Considering such a high complexity nature of the problem, we take advantage of a sufficient schedulability analysis, namely BCL analysis [7], which is the foundation of all the subsequent interference-based schedulability analyses. BCL analysis determines the schedulability of a given task set by checking if each task can be guaranteed its execution time within the deadline despite the maximum interference by higher priority jobs.

Anchoring on BCL analysis, we first observe the following trade-off relation when increasing the parallelization option for a task: For the task itself, its thread execution time becomes shorter and hence its tolerance for other tasks' interference gets larger. On the other hand, for other tasks, its larger parallelization option is disadvantageous since it can create a larger interference to other tasks. We formally model such trade-off relation between "tolerance" and "interference" as monotonic increasing functions of the parallelization option.

Leveraging those monotonic increasing properties, we propose a polynomial time algorithm that starts from no-parallelization for all the tasks and iteratively raises each task's parallelization option until the tolerance of every task becomes larger than the interference from other tasks. We formally prove that the proposed algorithm is optimal in terms of the BCL schedulability analysis, when the parallelization overhead is not significantly large. In addition, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated through both simulation and actual implementation. Our extensive experimental study says that the proposed algorithm can improve the schedulability up to 60%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to optimally enjoy the parallelization freedom in G-EDF. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents related work. Section III formally defines our problem of the parallelization option assignment. Section IV describes our extension of the BCL schedulability analysis considering the parallelization option. Then, Section V explains our proposed algorithm to optimally assign the parallelization options to the tasks. Section VI reports our experiment results. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: There have been numerous researches on real-time multicore scheduling with partitioned scheduling approaches [8]- [13] and global scheduling approaches including G-EDF [7], [14]- [19] and fluid scheduling [3]- [6], [20]- [26]. Also, many different task models are addressed, e.g., "multi-thread task model" [22], "fork-join task model" [16], [27], "multi-segment task model" [17], [26] and "DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) task model" [26]. However, all of them assume that each computational node is already parallelized into a prefixed number of threads.

In contrast, modern parallel programming frameworks such as OpenCL [1] and OpenMP [2] allow us to determine the number of threads a task is parallelized into, which creates the parallelization freedom of each task. Recent works [3], [4] address the optimal paralllelization problem targeting fluid scheduling such as PD 2 [5] and LLREF [6]. However, fluid scheduling is not commonly used in practice due to its enormous number of scheduler invocations and context switches.
Motivated by this limitation, in this paper, we address the optimal parallelization problem targeting more widely used G-EDF.

div.head: III. PROBLEM DESCRIPTION
div.p: We consider a system with m identical CPU cores and n sporadic tasks scheduled by G-EDF. Each sporadic task is denoted by τ k (1 ≤ k ≤ n) and the set of n sporadic tasks is denoted by Γ as follows:
div.formula: Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }. Each task τ k is represented as a 3-tuple, i.e., τ k = (T k , D k , E k )
div.p: where T k is the minimum inter-release time, D k is the relative deadline, and E k is the thread execution time table according to the parallelization option O k as shown in Fig. 2. For a task τ k , we can choose a parallelization option O k . The parallelization option O k ranges from 1 to O max = m meaning that we have options of parallelizing τ k into a single thread, i.e., O k = 1, two threads, i.e., O k = 2, and up to O max threads, i.e., O k = O max . If we choose the option O k for a task τ k , it means that the task is parallelized into O k sibling threads that share the same release times and deadlines. Thus, we denote such a parallelized task by τ k (O k ), which is the set of O k sibling threads, i.e.,
div.formula: τ k (O k ) = {τ 1 k (O k ), τ 2 k (O k ), • • • , τ O k k (O k )}, where τ l k (O k )(1 ≤ l ≤ O k ) is the l-th

div.p: . Also, the total computation amount or simply "computation amount" of O k sibling threads, i.e.,
div.formula: O k l=1 e l k (O k ), is denoted by C k (O k ): C k (O k ) = O k l=1 e l k (O k ).
div.p: In general, a larger parallelization option O k (> O k ) makes each of the thread execution time smaller, i.e., e l k (O k ) < e l k (O k ), but makes the computation amount larger, i.e.,
div.formula: C k (O k ) > C k (O k )
div.p: , due to the parallelization overhead.

For scheduling these n sporadic tasks on m identical CPU cores, we use G-EDF. Similar to other researches on G-EDF [7], [28]- [36], we assume that preemptions, migrations, and scheduling costs are either negligible or included in the WCET. Also, to focus on the scheduling aspect, we assume memory and bandwidth partitioning such as PALLOC [37] and MemGuard [38] to avoid inter-core interferences.

Under these assumptions, our problem is formally defined as follows: Problem Definition: For each task τ k in the given task set Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }, our problem is to find its parallelization option O k , such that all the sibling threads of all the tasks in Γ can be scheduled meeting their deadlines using G-EDF on m identical CPU cores.

div.head: IV. EXTENSION OF BCL SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR TASKS WITH PARALLELIZATION FREEDOM
div.p: To address our problem of the parallelization option assignment, we need a schedulability analysis. There have been various works on G-EDF schedulability analysis for sporadic task systems including exact analysis methods [36] and sufficient analysis methods [7], [28]- [35]. Although the exact analysis methods can be used to create the ground truth for the parallelization option assignment, they require exponential times and hence cannot be used for an online parallelization option assignment. Therefore, we use a sufficient analysis, namely BCL [7] analysis, as the basis for our online parallelization option assignment. Accordingly, our goal is to find an optimal algorithm for the parallelization option assignment in terms of the BCL schedulability analysis.
In this section, we first overview the BCL schedulability analysis and then show how it can be extended to determine the schedulability of tasks with the parallelization freedom.

div.head: A. Overview of BCL Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The BCL schedulability analysis belongs to a category of sufficient G-EDF schedulability analyses based on the concept of interference using the following definitions made by Bertogna et al. [7]:

Within the interval [a, b), regarding an interfered task τ k and an interfering task τ i 1) I τ k (a, b): Cumulative length of all intervals in which τ k is ready to execute but it cannot execute due to higher priority jobs. In other words, I τ k (a, b) involves all the intervals in which τ k is ready but all m CPU cores are occupied by other higher priority jobs (See Fig. 3). 2) I τi,τ k (a, b): Cumulative length of all intervals in which τ k is ready to execute but it cannot execute due to τ i 's jobs.

In other words, out of the cumulative intervals in I τ k (a, b), I τi,τ k (a, b) involves only intervals where τ i 's job is one of the higher priority jobs occupying the m CPU cores (See Fig. 3). From these definitions, for single-thread tasks,
div.formula: I τ k (a, b) is the summation of I τi,τ k (a, b) of all the interfering tasks τ i s (τ i ∈ Γ, τ i = τ k ) divided by m, i.e., I τ k (a, b) = 1 m τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) I τi,τ k (a, b).(1)
div.p: Using this, a schedulability condition can be derived for the j-th job of τ k , having the release time of r kj and the absolute deadline of d kj = r kj + D k . The job is schedulable when it can execute for its WCET denoted by e k inside its interval [r kj , d kj ). In other words, for the job not to miss the deadline, the interference should be smaller than or equal to D ke k . Combined with Eq. ( 1), this schedulability condition can be formulated as follows:
div.formula: I τk (r kj , d kj ) = 1 m τi∈Γ(τi =τk) I τi,τk (r kj , d kj ) ≤ D k -e k .(2)
div.p: However, Eq. ( 2) cannot be used directly, since it is difficult to calculate I τi,τ k (r kj , d kj ) values due to the vast number of possible execution scenarios of the sporadic tasks.

Instead, BCL and most other analyses use an upper bound of the interference I τi,τ k (r kj , d kj ). Such an upper bound is given by the total workload of the interfering task τ i within the interval [r kj , d kj ). Fig. 4 shows the worst-case release pattern of the interfering task τ i that gives the largest amount of workload into the interval of a τ k 's job in the G-EDF scheduling. It is when τ i 's last job's deadline coincides with the deadline of τ k 's job and τ i 's previous jobs are released most frequently, that is, with its minimum inter-release time T i . Considering this worst-case release pattern, the worst-case workload of τ i included in the interval of a τ k 's job, which is denoted by W τi,τ k , is given as follows:
div.formula: W τi,τ k = D k T i e i + min(e i , D k mod T i ).(3)
div.p: In this equation, the first term, i.e., D k Ti e i , is the workload by body jobs that are released and have deadlines within the interval of a τ k 's job. The second term, i.e., min(e i , D k mod T i ), is the workload by a carry-in job that are released before the interval but has its deadline within the interval. This worst-case workload W τi,τ k , from now on, is simply called "workload from τ i to τ k ".

Since the interference I τi,τ k (r kj , d kj ) cannot be greater than the workload W τi,τ k , the schedulability condition in Eq. ( 2) can be transformed into a sufficient schedulability condition as follows:
div.formula: I τ k (r kj , d kj ) = 1 m τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) I τi,τ k (r kj , d kj ) ≤ 1 m τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) W τi,τ k ≤ D k -e k .(4)
div.p: This sufficient schedulability condition gets more tightened in the BCL schedulability analysis by introducing "bounded workload", denoted W τi,τ k , as a tighter upper bound of the interference I τi,τ k (r kj , d kj ). That is, for a job of τ k to be schedulable, it should be interfered by τ i not more than D ke k . Thus, we can limit the workload W τi,τ k by D ke k when considering the interference from τ i for the schedulability of a τ k 's job, which results in the following bounded workload:
div.formula: W τi,τ k = min(W τi,τ k , D k -e k ).(5)
div.p: We call W τi,τ k "bounded workload from τ i to τ k " or "interference from τ i to τ k ", whenever there is no ambiguity. By replacing W τi,τ k in Eq. ( 4) with a tighter upper bound, that is, the bounded workload W τi,τ k in Eq. ( 5) and moving m to the right-hand side, we finally have the following BCL schedulability condition for each task τ k :
div.formula: τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) W τi,τ k = τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) min(W τi,τ k , D k -e k ) ≤ m(D k -e k ).(6)
div.p: In addition, the BCL schedulability condition enforces that at most m -1 interfering tasks τ i s have workloads W τi,τ k s exceeding D ke k . This is because if m or more τ i s have workloads exceeding D ke k , there can be a case where τ k cannot be guaranteed e k from its release time to its absolute deadline [7].

From now on, by the "schedulability" of a task τ k , we mean that τ k meets this BCL sufficient schedulability condition. Also, when we say that the given task set Γ is schedulable, it means that the BCL condition holds for every task τ k ∈ Γ.

div.head: B. BCL Extension and Properties for Tasks with Parallelization Freedom

However, note that sibling threads have a clear difference from non-sibling threads. This algorithm can be formally described as the pseudo codes in Algorithm 1. The algorithm takes the set of tasks Γ as input and produces the parallelization option combination O, if any, that makes the given task set schedulable, as output. The for-loop from Line 1 to Line 5 pre-calculates the tolerance W tolerance τ k (O k ) for each task τ k ∈ Γ and for each option O k (≤ O max ) using Eq. ( 10) as in Fig. 8(a). In Line 6, we create an array S where each element S k ∈ S is initialized to Unknown, meaning the schedulability of τ k is yet unknown. Then, Line 7 initializes the parallelization options to O cur = (1, 1, ..., 1) and Line 8 sets the "updated" flag as true. Then, the while-loop from Line 9 to Line 24 iteratively increases the parallelization options to the barely tolerable ones until it turns out "schedulable" or "not schedulable". For this, in each iteration of the while-loop, Line 10 first resets the updated flag to false, meaning that we will terminate the while-loop if no parallelization option is updated. Then Line 11 sets the previous parallelization option combination O pre the same as the current option combination O cur . Then, the for-loop from Line 12 to Line 22 tries to update each task τ k 's parallelization option O cur k to the barely tolerable ones as in Fig. 8(b). For this, within the for-loop, Line 13 calculates the total interference given to τ k , i.e., τi∈Γ(τi =τ k ) W interference τi,τ k (O pre i ), using Eq. ( 12) with the previous parallelization options. Then, the while-loop from Line 14 to Line 21 checks whether τ k 's tolerance is smaller than the interference from other tasks. If so, Line 15 increases O cur k to the next one and Line 16 sets the updated flag as true indicating that some options are updated. This is repeated until the barely tolerable option is found. In the meantime, however, if O cur k becomes larger than O max as in Line 17, it means that τ k 's tolerance even with O max is still smaller than the interference from other tasks and hence τ k is unschedulable. In this case, Line 18 marks S k as false and sets O cur k = O max . Line 19 then breaks the while-loop from Line 14 to Line 21 and goes back to Line 12 to continue with unchecked tasks for finding their barely tolerable options. After checking all the tasks in the current iteration, Line 23 checks if there is a task that turns out unschedulable and if so it breaks the while-loop from Line 9 to Line 24. When the while-loop from Line 9 to Line 24 terminates, the ifelse statement from Line 25 to Line 29 returns the "not schedulable" or "schedulable" conclusion. When the given task set is schedulable, it also returns the found parallelization option combination O cur .

div.head: B. The time complexity of Algorithm 1
div.p: Instead of a back-and-forth combinatorial search, Algorithm 1 conducts a one-way search in the outer while-loop from Line 9 to Line 24 by leveraging the monotonic increasing property of both tolerance and interference. Thus, for n tasks with the constant number O max of parallelization options, the number of options increases is at most n • O max and hence O(n). For each of such increases, the algorithm may calculate the interference in Line 13 with the time complexity of O(n) for all n tasks by the for-loop from Line 12 to Line 22. This becomes O(n 2 ) time complexity. Thus, the overall time complexity of the algorithm is O(n 3 ).

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENT RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we show the effectiveness of the proposed task parallelization algorithm by both simulation with synthetic tasks and actual implementation with real autonomous driving tasks.

With such generated 10 6 task sets and four CPU cores, i.e, m = 4, we compare the schedulability resulting from the following four different parallelization approaches:
• Ours: Each task parallelized using our proposed algorithm, i.e., Algorithm 1. • Random: For each task τ k , the parallelization option is randomly chosen from uniform[1, O max ].

Fig. 10(a) compares the schedulability of the above four approaches for the whole spectrum of the task set utilization of 10 6 task sets ranging from 0 to 4 assuming the parallelization overhead α(O k , O k + 1) = 0.3 for every O k < O max = 4. In the figure, the x-axis represents the task set utilization and the y-axis represents the schedulability, i.e., the proportion of schedulable task sets out of all the task sets having the corresponding task set utilization. Comparing "Max" and "Single", the former performs better in low task set utilization while the latter performs better in high task set utilization making a crossing point around the task set utilization of 1.3. This is because in low utilization the schedulability is mostly affected by deadlines and hence reducing the thread execution time by parallelization helps. On the other hand, in high utilization, the schedulability is mostly affected by the amount of interferences among tasks and hence keeping the number of threads small helps. "Random" is between "Max" and "Single". "Ours" performs significantly better in any task set utilization, e.g., 60% more schedulable task sets at the crossing point of "Max" and "Single" ‡ . This is because Algorithm 1 optimally trades-off the tolerance and interference in the parallelization option selection for the schedulability of all the tasks in the given task set. Fig. 10(b) shows the results when the parallelization overhead is larger, i.e., when α(O k , O k + 1) = 0.8. In this case, "Single" is not affected but "Max" becomes worse since the benefit by parallelization is severely sacrificed due to the large parallelization overhead. "Ours" is similarly affected. Nevertheless, "Ours" still significantly outperforms all other approaches in this case of large parallelization overhead. Fig. 10(c) shows the results when the deadline for each task is 20% tighter than Fig. 10(a). In this case, "Single" becomes significantly worse because it does not take advantage of thread execution time reduction by parallelization. On the other hand, the performance of "Max" and "Random" also drop but not that much compared with "Single" thanks to ‡ By applying the improved interference based schedulability analysis called RTA [33] to "Single", "Max", and "Random", our experiments say that their schedulability improve, but less than 5%. the parallelization. The performance of "Ours" just slightly drops since it can well overcome the tightened deadlines by the optimal parallelization.

div.head: B. Implementation Results
div.p: For the practical justification of our proposed approach, we implemented a set of real-time tasks using PREEMPT RT patched on top of Linux kernel 4.19. The tasks are scheduled according to G-EDF (SCHED DEADLINE) scheduler on a PC equipped with Intel Core i7-8700 CPU (6-cores). We use CPUSET to limit the execution of our tasks into m = 4 cores, fix the clock frequency at 3.20 GHz, and disable GPU.

On this framework, we execute the following four real programs used for autonomous driving, i.e., (1) τ 1 : sensor read program emulating a multi-channel camera module, (2) τ 2 : lane tracking program used by Autoware [40], (3) τ 3 : darknet [41]-based object detection and labeling program used by APOLLO [42], and (4) τ 4 : steering actuation program emulating PID motor controller. Their minimum inter-release times and deadlines are set as (T 1 = D 1 = 20, 000), (T 2 = D 2 = 150, 000), (T 3 = D 3 = 120, 000), and (T 4 = D 4 = 20, 000), where the time unit is μs.

Fig. 11 shows the measured response times of the largest thread τ 1 k (O k ) of each task τ k . In each graph, the x-axis is the release time of each job and the y-axis is its corresponding response time. The horizontal line on each graph is the deadline D k and thus the response time above it means a deadline violation. In "Single", we can observe many deadline misses of τ 2 and τ 3 . This is because they are time-taking tasks and hence without parallelization, their execution times are longer than the deadlines pretty often. In "Max" and "Random", the number of τ 2 's and τ 3 's deadline misses decrease thanks to the parallelization but now we observe deadline misses of the short tasks τ 1 and τ 4 due to increased interferences. On the other hand, we can observe that "Ours" meet all the deadlines of all the four tasks by the optimal parallelization.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we present an optimal parallelization of realtime tasks for G-EDF. For this, we extend the BCL sufficient schedulability analysis for the tasks with the parallelization freedom and model the tolerance and the interference as Leveraging their monotonic increasing properties, we propose an optimal parallelization algorithm with polynomial time complexity. Through both simulation and actual implementation, we show both significant schedulability improvement and practicality of our proposed approach.

In the future, we plan to extend our approach to other stateof-the-art schedulability analyses. We also plan to extend this work for other task models such as the multi-segment task model and the DAG task model.
